title: Antonito Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Antonito wells have a 61-foot median depth; see yields, water levels, drilling costs, permits, and risks before buying rural property.
h1: Antonito, Colorado Well Depths, Yields, and Costs
intro_html:
Buying land or a home near Antonito means understanding the well record before you rely on a listing description. Within 5 miles of Antonito, Colorado, DWR permit records include 981 wells. Of those, 705 are recorded as constructed, 689 report total depth, 137 report pump yield, and 63 report a static water level.

The local records point to generally shallow wells with solid reported production, but the spread is wide. A specific lot can still encounter different ground, a deeper water-bearing zone, or an incomplete permit history. Use nearby wells as a starting point, then confirm the site with a licensed driller, water-quality testing, and a review of the permit and well construction documents.

sections.heading: Antonito well depths reflect shallow valley ground
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Antonito is 61 feet, and the middle half runs from 40 to 120 feet. That is a useful starting point for a drilling estimate, not a guarantee for a particular parcel. Sixty-six percent of recorded wells are under 100 feet, while 27% fall from 100 to 300 feet. Six percent are 300 to 600 feet, and 1% are deeper than 600 feet.

The 90th-percentile depth is 258 feet, and the deepest record reaches 771 feet. Permits identify the unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer on 927 wells, with additional records in the Unconfined San Luis Valley aquifer units. Mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground can drill easily in one location and change quickly across a short distance, so a driller should review nearby logs before bidding.

sections.heading: What Antonito wells report for yield
sections.html:
Reported pump yields are favorable overall, although only 137 wells include a yield in the records. The median is 14.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 10.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Fifty percent report between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, while 48% report more than 15 gallons per minute. One percent report from 1 to 5 gallons per minute, and no reported wells are under 1 gallon per minute.

For a buyer, that suggests the local records are not dominated by marginal production. It does not mean every new hole will make 14.0 gallons per minute. Yield depends on the screened or fractured zone, construction, pump testing, and seasonal conditions. Ask for the well completion report and a sustained yield test rather than relying on a verbal estimate or a neighboring parcel alone.

sections.heading: Antonito water levels and the recent record
sections.html:
Among the 63 wells reporting static water level, the median depth to water is 60 feet. The middle half ranges from 30 to 150 feet below the surface. That range matters for pump selection, trench planning, and the amount of lift a system may need, even where the drilled hole itself is shallow.

The decade comparison does not show a deeper reported water table in the available series. The median static water level is 60 feet below surface for measurements in the 2010s and 52 feet in the 2020s, meaning the later reported median is shallower by 8 feet. This is not a promise that water levels will rise at your property. It is a limited permit-record snapshot, so request current testing when the water supply is important to the purchase.

sections.heading: Who has drilled near Antonito, and when
sections.html:
Permit activity extends across several generations. Records show 11 permits in the 1950s, 12 in the 1960s, 140 in the 1970s, 114 in the 1980s, 99 in the 1990s, 203 in the 2000s, 115 in the 2010s, and 70 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025. Older wells may have incomplete construction, pump, or water-level information, so age matters when comparing them with a proposed new well.

The most active drillers in these records are Heersink Drilling, also listed as Heersink, Scott, with 93 wells; Valley Pump Company, listed as Self, Clinton L., with 78; and Larry Burk Drilling, listed as Burk, Larry, with 44. These counts describe permit records, not current availability or an endorsement. Confirm licensing, insurance, scheduling, and the scope of a current bid directly.

sections.heading: A practical Antonito well drilling budget
sections.html:
The local cost model uses a typical drilling rate of $50 to $75 per foot in mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground. At the 61-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $3,000 to $4,600. That figure is only the hole. It does not represent a ready-to-use household water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at about $9,000 to $16,600 at the median depth. A deeper-than-typical hole, difficult access, casing or grouting requirements, additional trench length, or a different pump arrangement can move the final price. Have the driller state what is included, the assumed depth, testing, casing, grout, permits, electrical work, and the price if the first hole is dry or produces less than expected.

sections.heading: Antonito risks to check before construction
sections.html:
Low yield is not the leading pattern in the reported records, but a record cannot guarantee production on an untested lot. Dry holes, poor water quality, inadequate casing or grout, and pump problems remain practical risks. The aquifer descriptions are heavily weighted toward unnamed or fractured-bedrock records, where water can be unevenly distributed. A good pre-purchase review includes neighboring well depths, completion reports, static levels, pump yields, and any available laboratory water tests.

Environmental records within about 10 miles include 1 PFAS sampling or contamination site, 0 historic mine features, and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. That does not establish contamination at a particular address, but it supports testing before occupancy. Also confirm septic setbacks, replacement-area requirements, driveway access, building-envelope constraints, and the legal use allowed by the DWR permit. Domestic, household, and stock uses dominate the records; irrigation appears on 5% of permits.

sections.heading: Before buying an Antonito lot or home
sections.html:
Start with the exact parcel, not just the Antonito area. Pull the DWR permit, construction report, well location, pump information, and any recorded water-quality results. Compare the property with nearby wells in Antonito and toward Conejos, then look at records around Romeo, Manassa, Sanford, La Jara, and Capulin only as broader context because ground conditions can change.

For an existing home, make the sale conditional on inspecting the well, pressure system, storage, electrical supply, and septic system, followed by water-quality and flow testing. For vacant land, obtain a written drilling proposal and confirm access for the rig, space for the well and septic system, and the intended permit use before finalizing site plans. Colorado DWR approval and any augmentation requirements should be checked before assuming a proposed use is available.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Antonito, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Antonito is 61 feet. The middle half runs from 40 to 120 feet, while the 90th-percentile depth is 258 feet. Sixty-six percent of recorded wells are under 100 feet, but the deepest record reaches 771 feet, so a parcel-specific estimate still requires nearby logs and a driller’s review.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Antonito?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $50 to $75 per foot. At the 61-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $3,000 to $4,600. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is about $9,000 to $16,600. Soil, access, depth, casing, testing, and a dry or low-yield hole can change the final bid.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Antonito?
faq.a: Among the 137 wells that report pump yield, the median is 14.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 10.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Fifty percent report 5 to 15 gallons per minute, and 48% report more than 15 gallons per minute. These figures describe recorded tests, not a guaranteed result for a new well.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Antonito?
faq.a: The permit records do not establish that every well is safe to drink. Test the property’s water through a qualified laboratory, especially before occupancy. Within about 10 miles, records show 1 PFAS sampling or contamination site and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. Those locations do not prove contamination at your address, but they make testing and site review sensible.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping near Antonito?
faq.a: The available static-level series does not show a deeper reported median water table. The median was 60 feet below surface for measurements in the 2010s and 52 feet in the 2020s, so the later reported median was 8 feet shallower. Only 63 wells report static water level, however, so this record should not replace current testing at the property.
